title: The verb forms in discourse, and ambiguities

objectives.can: Describe what qatal, yiqtol, wayyiqtol, weqatal and the participle each tend to do in narrative, in speech and in poetry, and state the main points on which scholars disagree.

explanation.summary: Hebrew verb forms do not map neatly onto English tenses, and scholars have described them in three main ways: as tenses, as aspects, and as forms with jobs in discourse. Each account explains much and none explains everything. This lesson sets out what each form tends to do, where it can be read in more than one way, and what the disagreements are.

sections.heading: Three accounts of the system
body: The tense account holds that the qatal refers to the past and the yiqtol to the future, with the wayyiqtol as the past of narrative. It is the account of the oldest teaching and fits many verses. It has trouble with the many places where a qatal speaks of the present or future, or a yiqtol of the past.

The aspect account, associated with S. R. Driver and the grammars that followed him, holds that the forms show how the speaker looks at an action: as a complete whole (the qatal) or as something not complete, in progress, repeated or still ahead (the yiqtol). It explains why the same form can serve for several times. Critics say that aspect is a description the scholar imposes, since the forms are used in ways that no single viewpoint covers.

The discourse account asks what a form does in a text. A wayyiqtol chain carries the main line of a story, a qatal beginning a clause with another word gives background, and a weqatal carries on a line of instructions or predictions. It explains the sequence of forms well. It does not by itself say what a form means in an isolated sentence.
Each account captures part of the truth, and many modern grammars combine them. The right habit for a reader is to know what each form tends to do, and to say 'tends' when describing it.

sections.heading: What each form tends to do
body: Qatal: in narrative it often reports a completed event, and, when placed after a subject or another word, a background or earlier event. With verbs of state or of the mind it often speaks of the present: יָדַעְתִּי is 'I know' (literally, I have come to know). In speech it can be a past, a present result or, in promises, a certainty.

Yiqtol: in speech it often looks ahead (תָּמוּת, 'you will die'). It also describes what is habitual or general, in the past as well as in the present, and what is modal, 'may', 'should', 'would'. Which of these is meant comes from the context.

Wayyiqtol: in narrative it is the form that moves the story on, one event after another. Many scholars connect it with an older short past form and regard the וַ as part of that form rather than as the word 'and'.

Weqatal: it carries on what a yiqtol, an imperative or another forward-looking form began: instructions, predictions and general statements. In past narrative a weqatal can describe a repeated action.
Participle: it describes an action in progress or a state, with no time of its own. The context makes it present, past or about to happen.

sections.heading: Speech, narrative and poetry
body: In prose narrative the pattern is a chain of wayyiqtols with the occasional qatal for background. In speech the forms shift: qatal for what is done or true, yiqtol for what will be or should be, participles for what is under way, weqatal for the sequel to a command or a prediction.

In poetry the forms are freer. The two halves of a line may use different forms for the same time, and a yiqtol can refer to the past where prose would have used a wayyiqtol. Exodus 15:1 begins with אָז and a yiqtol, and is usually read as past, 'then Moses sang', though a future reading has also been held in some traditions. The lesson on poetry returns to this.

sections.heading: Ambiguities a reader must weigh
body: The yiqtol: future, habitual or modal. Genesis 2:6, וְאֵד יַעֲלֶה, can be read as a habitual 'a mist used to rise' or as a plain background statement about the past; the form does not decide.

The qatal of speech: in Genesis 1:29 the form נָתַתִּי can be read as a past, 'I have given', or as a performative, 'I hereby give', in which the saying is itself the giving. Most grammars accept performatives in cases like Genesis 23:11, where the speaker is conveying the field by speaking. In Genesis 1:29 the choice is not forced, and translations differ.

The prophetic perfect: a qatal used of an event still to come, as if already done, is a category found in many grammars. In Isaiah 9:5 the forms יֻלַּד and נִתַּן, 'is born' and 'is given', are read by some as certain future events, and by others as present or recent events celebrated by the prophet. Some scholars doubt that 'prophetic perfect' is a separate use; they prefer to explain such verses by the discourse setting.

Long and short forms: the short yiqtol is used for wishes and prohibitions (the jussive), and in many verbs it looks exactly like the long one. In אַל יִחַר, 'let him not be angry', the form is the same as a plain yiqtol; the negative אַל shows that it is volitive. A reader has to use the particle or the context.

misunderstandings: The qatal is not simply 'the past tense' and the yiqtol is not simply 'the future'. They tend that way, and there are many exceptions.
The wayyiqtol does not mean 'and he' plus a yiqtol. Its past sense in narrative is part of its use, and the grammars explain its history in different ways.
A qatal about the future is not a mistake. Whether to call it a prophetic perfect, a performative or a use of a discourse setting is a matter of interpretation.
Choosing a translation is not the same as stating the grammar. A verse may be translated in one way and still allow a second reading.

deeper.heading: The old short past and the wayyiqtol
body: Comparison with other Semitic languages suggests that an old short past form lies behind the Hebrew wayyiqtol, and that the short jussive is a relative of it. If so, the likeness between the jussive and the wayyiqtol in verbs like 'be' (יְהִי, 'let there be'; וַיְהִי, 'and there was') is not an accident. This is a comparative argument; it explains a pattern in the forms, and it does not settle which description of the system is best.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it; for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The yiqtol לֹא תֹאכַל is a prohibition and the yiqtol תָּמוּת, with the infinitive absolute, a warning of what will follow. Both look ahead. This is the yiqtol's commonest speech sense, and it is a case where the tense account and the aspect account both work.

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: And this man went up out of his city from year to year to worship and to sacrifice unto the LORD of hosts in Shiloh. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there priests unto the LORD.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The first verb, וְעָלָה, is a weqatal in a story about the past. It does not tell of one event but of a custom: 'that man used to go up from his city year after year'. The weqatal here carries a habit, and the time comes from the narrative frame and from the phrase 'from year to year'.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: 'Nay, my lord, hear me: the field give I thee, and the cave that is therein, I give it thee; in the presence of the sons of my people give I it thee; bury thy dead.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The verb נְתַתִּיהָ and the earlier נָתַתִּי are qatals, but Ephron is not reporting an earlier gift. He is making the gift as he speaks. Most grammars call this a performative use: 'I give you the field', with the saying as the act.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two forms of the same verb. יְהִי is the short form, a jussive, 'let there be'. וַיְהִי is the wayyiqtol of narrative, 'and there was'. The wish is spoken and the story reports the result. The two forms are close in spelling, which is the comparative point noted under the deeper heading.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods; yea, for that they dealt proudly against them.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: יָדַעְתִּי is a qatal of knowing, and the verb is best taken as a present, 'I know', since it describes a state that has just come about. The particle עַתָּה, 'now', shows that. A tense account that says 'qatal is past' would need to say 'I knew'; an aspect account explains that the state is seen as complete and therefore present.

practice.prompt: What time does the yiqtol תָּמוּת (word 12) most naturally refer to?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it; for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The future: a warning of what will follow on the day
practice.explain: In a warning the yiqtol looks ahead, and the infinitive absolute before it adds certainty. The same form is used in other places for habit or for modal senses, so the context has to decide.

practice.prompt: What does the yiqtol יַעֲשֶׂה (word 1) most naturally express in this verse?

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: And as he did so year by year, when she went up to the house of the LORD, so she vexed her; therefore she wept, and would not eat.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A repeated action in the past: this is what used to happen year after year
practice.explain: The phrase 'year after year' shows that the yiqtol, here and in תַּכְעִסֶנָּה, is habitual in a past setting. The form does not itself say 'past'; the context does.

practice.prompt: How can the qatal נָתַתִּי (word 4) be read in Ephron's speech?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: 'Nay, my lord, hear me: the field give I thee, and the cave that is therein, I give it thee; in the presence of the sons of my people give I it thee; bury thy dead.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Only as a report of an earlier gift
As a performative: in saying it, he gives the field
practice.explain: Ephron is not saying that he gave the field before; he is offering it now. The speech act is the giving. Most grammars take a qatal used so as a performative.

practice.prompt: What time does the qatal יָדַעְתִּי (word 1) refer to?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods; yea, for that they dealt proudly against them.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The present: 'I know', a state that has come about
practice.explain: A qatal of knowing often describes the present state that results from having learned. The word עַתָּה, 'now', points the same way.

practice.prompt: How does the reader know that אַל־יִשְׁתּוּ (words 17 and 18) is volitive, though the form is spelled like a plain yiqtol?

quoted.title: Jonah
quoted.english: And he caused it to be proclaimed and published through Nineveh by the decree of the king and his nobles, saying: 'Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, taste any thing; let them not feed, nor drink water;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: By the ending alone, which is always short
By the vowel, which cannot be a yiqtol's
By the particle אַל, which goes with the jussive in a prohibition
practice.explain: For many verbs the short and the long forms look alike. The negative אַל, used for a negative wish or command, is the sign. The king's decree says 'let them not drink'.

check.prompt: Which statement is grammatically possible for the yiqtol of אָז יָשִׁיר (words 0 and 1)?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD, and spoke, saying: I will sing unto the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Past or future: the yiqtol in poetry after אָז is usually read as a past, 'then Moses sang', but a future reading has been held
Only a future: they will sing
check.explain: In older poetry a yiqtol can refer to the past, and the majority read the verse so, since the song follows an event just told. The form alone does not settle it, and the future reading has had its defenders in the tradition.

check.prompt: How can the qatals יֻלַּד and נִתַּן (words 2 and 5) be read in this verse?

quoted.title: Isaiah
quoted.english: For a child is born unto us, a son is given unto us; and the government is upon his shoulder; and his name is called Pele-joez-el-gibbor-Abi-ad-sar-shalom;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: As events that have just happened or are present to the prophet, or as future events spoken of as certain (a so-called prophetic perfect); the form does not decide
check.explain: Both readings are advanced by interpreters. The prophetic perfect is a recognised label, though some scholars prefer to explain the verse by its setting. The grammar permits each.

check.prompt: What are the weqatal verbs וְדָבַק and וְהָיוּ (words 8 and 10) doing after the yiqtol יַעֲזָב?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife, and they shall be one flesh.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: They carry on a general statement begun by the yiqtol: what a man does, and what follows
They narrate a past event in sequence
They are commands to the woman
check.explain: A weqatal continues a forward-looking or general statement. The writer states a custom in the present of the narrator, with the yiqtol first and the weqatals continuing it. The two accounts, tense and discourse, can both describe it.

check.prompt: What does the weqatal וְעָלָה (word 0) show in a story about the past?

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: And this man went up out of his city from year to year to worship and to sacrifice unto the LORD of hosts in Shiloh. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there priests unto the LORD.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A repeated custom: the man used to go up every year
A single event that happened once
check.explain: The phrase 'from year to year' and the setting show that the verb describes a habit. A weqatal is the form often used for a repeated action of this kind in past narrative.

check.prompt: Which readings of נָתַתִּי (word 3) are grammatically possible?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God said: 'Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed — to you it shall be for food;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A past, 'I have given', or a performative, 'I hereby give'; translations differ and the form does not decide
check.explain: God speaks, and his speech makes the gift. A performative reading fits that, but 'I have given' is also possible, taking the gift as already made. Both are within the grammar.

check.prompt: What does the qatal חָשַׂכְתָּ (word 18) look back on?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And he said: 'Lay not thy hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him; for now I know that thou art a God-fearing man, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son, from Me.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A completed act that has just been done and from which the speaker draws his conclusion: you have not withheld your son
check.explain: The qatal reports what Abraham has done, and the first clause, עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי, draws the consequence now. This is the qatal in its plain use for a completed action with present relevance.

check.prompt: What does אֶעֱשֶׂה (word 12) express in 'לֹא אֶעֱשֶׂה'?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And he said: 'Oh, let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak. Peradventure there shall thirty be found there.' And He said: 'I will not do it, if I find thirty there.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The speaker's own future or resolve: 'I will not do it', where the yiqtol is a promise
check.explain: The yiqtol of the first person naturally looks ahead. Whether it is called a plain future or an expression of resolve is a matter of how one describes it; the sense is clear.

check.prompt: What is the difference between יְהִי (word 2) and וַיְהִי (word 4)?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: יְהִי is a short volitive (jussive), 'let there be', and וַיְהִי a narrative wayyiqtol, 'and there was'
יְהִי is past and וַיְהִי future
check.explain: The wish is spoken, and the story reports its result with the wayyiqtol. The two forms are alike in their letters, which supports the comparative view that they have a common source.

check.prompt: How can the yiqtol יַעֲלֶה (word 1) be read in this verse?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: but there went up a mist from the earth, and watered the whole face of the ground.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: As a habitual or repeated action in the past ('a mist used to rise'), or as a plain background statement; the form does not decide
check.explain: A yiqtol after a subject, in a clause that describes the scene, can be taken as habitual or as simple background. The tense account would struggle here, as would any account that read the yiqtol as only future.

check.prompt: What time do the yiqtols יִתֵּן and יִבּוֹל (words 8 and 12) describe?

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: And he shall be like a tree planted by streams of water, that bringeth forth its fruit in its season, and whose leaf doth not wither; and in whatsoever he doeth he shall prosper.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A general, repeated truth about the tree and the man it stands for
check.explain: The psalm describes what is true as a rule, in a simile. The yiqtol is the usual form for such general statements, which are neither past nor future in particular.

check.prompt: Which statement fairly summarises the discourse account of the verb forms?
options: Each form has one tense and no other
A form is best described by the job it does in a text, such as carrying the main line of a story or giving background, and this explains the order of forms in a passage
The forms have no regular use
Only the wayyiqtol has any meaning
check.explain: The discourse account asks what a form does in its text. It explains sequences of forms well, and it does not claim to give each form a single meaning in isolation. The tense and aspect accounts each describe part of the same evidence.

reading.why: The second creation account mixes the forms: yiqtols after טֶרֶם in verse 5 for what had not yet come about, a qatal in the same verse for the cause (the LORD had not sent rain), a habitual or background yiqtol in verse 6, and wayyiqtols that carry the story from verse 7. The passage lets you ask, form by form, whether tense, aspect or function explains it best.
